claim: Loss of polarity correlates with progression of epithelial cancers.
source: Loss of polarity correlates with progression of epithelial cancers, but how plasma membrane misorganization drives oncogenic transcriptional events remains unclear.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established scientific understanding about cancer progression.

claim: The polarity regulators of the Drosophila Scribble (Scrib) module are potent tumor suppressors.
source: The polarity regulators of the Drosophila Scribble (Scrib) module are potent tumor suppressors and provide a model for mechanistic investigation.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental work described in the manuscript and references to prior research.

claim: RNA profiling of Scrib mutant tumors reveals multiple signatures of neoplasia, including altered metabolism and dedifferentiation.
source: RNA profiling of Scrib mutant tumors reveals multiple signatures of neoplasia, including altered metabolism and dedifferentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-Seq data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 1 and associated supplementary files.

claim: Upregulation of cytokine-like Unpaired (Upd) ligands drives tumor overgrowth in Scrib mutant tumors.
source: Prominent among these is upregulation of cytokine-like Unpaired (Upd) ligands, which drive tumor overgrowth.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-Seq data showing upd gene upregulation and functional experiments showing that JAK/STAT pathway inhibition suppresses overgrowth.

claim: A polarity-responsive enhancer in upd3 is activated in a coincident manner by both JNK-dependent Fos and aPKC-mediated Yki transcription.
source: We identified a polarity-responsive enhancer in upd3, which is activated in a coincident manner by both JNK-dependent Fos and aPKC-mediated Yki transcription.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that both JNK/Fos and aPKC/Yki pathways are required for full enhancer activation, as shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The upd3 enhancer and Scrib mutant overgrowth are sensitive to activity of the Polycomb Group (PcG).
source: This enhancer, and Scrib mutant overgrowth in general, are also sensitive to activity of the Polycomb Group (PcG), suggesting that PcG attenuation upon polarity loss potentiates select targets for activation by JNK and Yki.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that PcG knockdown enhances neoplastic growth and that PcG mutants activate the upd3.3 enhancer, as shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: PcG attenuation upon polarity loss potentiates select targets for activation by JNK and Yki.
source: This enhancer, and Scrib mutant overgrowth in general, are also sensitive to activity of the Polycomb Group (PcG), suggesting that PcG attenuation upon polarity loss potentiates select targets for activation by JNK and Yki.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the genetic interaction experiments and transcriptome comparisons.

claim: Pronounced disorganization of biopsied epithelia is well-established to correlate with tumor malignancy and lethality.
source: Pronounced disorganization of biopsied epithelia is well-established to correlate with tumor malignancy and lethality.
evidence: This reflects established clinical and pathological knowledge about cancer diagnosis.

claim: The apical determinant atypical protein kinase C (aPKC) is amplified and over-expressed in multiple cancers.
source: For instance, the apical determinant atypical protein kinase C (aPKC) is amplified and over-expressed in multiple cancers (Huang and Muthuswamy, 2010; Parker et al., 2014), while basolateral regulators are altered in several tumor types and degraded by viral oncoproteins (Huang and Muthuswamy, 2010; Elsum et al., 2012); cancer stem cell activity may also be promoted by transition from an epithelial state (Martin-Belmonte and Perez-Moreno, 2011; Scheel and Weinberg, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Basolateral regulators are altered in several tumor types and degraded by viral oncoproteins.
source: For instance, the apical determinant atypical protein kinase C (aPKC) is amplified and over-expressed in multiple cancers (Huang and Muthuswamy, 2010; Parker et al., 2014), while basolateral regulators are altered in several tumor types and degraded by viral oncoproteins (Huang and Muthuswamy, 2010; Elsum et al., 2012); cancer stem cell activity may also be promoted by transition from an epithelial state (Martin-Belmonte and Perez-Moreno, 2011; Scheel and Weinberg, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Cancer stem cell activity may be promoted by transition from an epithelial state.
source: For instance, the apical determinant atypical protein kinase C (aPKC) is amplified and over-expressed in multiple cancers (Huang and Muthuswamy, 2010; Parker et al., 2014), while basolateral regulators are altered in several tumor types and degraded by viral oncoproteins (Huang and Muthuswamy, 2010; Elsum et al., 2012); cancer stem cell activity may also be promoted by transition from an epithelial state (Martin-Belmonte and Perez-Moreno, 2011; Scheel and Weinberg, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Scribble (scrib), discs-large (dlg), and lethal giant larvae (lgl) cooperatively distinguish the basolateral domain from the apical by antagonizing aPKC activity.
source: These polarity regulators–scribble (scrib), discs-large (dlg), and lethal giant larvae (lgl)- cooperatively distinguish the basolateral domain from the apical by antagonizing aPKC activity (St Johnston and Ahringer, 2010; Tepass, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on polarity regulation.

claim: The conserved 'Scrib module' functions in both vertebrates and invertebrates, not only in epithelia but also other polarized cell types.
source: This conserved 'Scrib module' functions in both vertebrates and invertebrates, not only in epithelia but also other polarized cell types.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the conservation and function of the Scrib module.

claim: When Scrib module function is lost from fly epithelia, mutant cells round up and become multilayered.
source: When Scrib module function is lost from fly epithelia, mutant cells round up and become multilayered.
evidence: This is a well-established phenotype of Scrib module mutants, supported by the images in Figure 1.

claim: In imaginal discs, Scrib module mutant tissue continuously proliferates to more than five times the WT cell number before it kills the animal.
source: In the imaginal discs, epithelial organs which normally have a precise intrinsic size-control mechanism, mutant tissue continuously proliferates to more than five times the WT cell number before it kills the animal.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation about the overgrowth phenotype of Scrib module mutants.

claim: Small portions of neoplastic tumorous mass, when transplanted into adults, continue to grow uncontrollably and kill the host.
source: Small portions of the tumorous mass, when transplanted into adults, continue to grow uncontrollably and kill the host; such allografts can be repeated indefinitely.
evidence: This describes the transplantability phenotype of neoplastic tissue, a classic characteristic.

claim: Neoplastic fly tissue is prone to dissemination and degrades basement membrane.
source: Neoplastic fly tissue is prone to dissemination and degrades basement membrane; in cooperation with oncogenic Ras it can migrate away from its primary site and invade other organs (Pagliarini and Xu, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: In cooperation with oncogenic Ras, neoplastic tissue can migrate away from its primary site and invade other organs.
source: Neoplastic fly tissue is prone to dissemination and degrades basement membrane; in cooperation with oncogenic Ras it can migrate away from its primary site and invade other organs (Pagliarini and Xu, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Neoplastic tissue is compromised in its differentiation potential, and cannot form adult structures.
source: It is compromised in its differentiation potential, and cannot form adult structures (Gateff and Schneiderman, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Neoplastic tissue can be recognized by the host innate immune system, whose cellular activities impede its growth.
source: It can be recognized by the host innate immune system, whose cellular activities impede its growth (Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008; Cordero et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Neoplastic tissue produces long-range signals that induce detrimental responses in fly hosts, including cachexia-like tissue wasting.
source: Finally, it produces long-range signals that induce detrimental responses in fly hosts, including cachexia-like tissue wasting (Figueroa-Clarevega and Bilder, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: RNA-Seq analysis identified 574 genes misregulated at least twofold in both scrib and dlg tumors (FDR <5%), with 311 upregulated and 263 downregulated.
source: Analysis revealed 574 genes misregulated at least twofold in both mutant tissues (FDR <5%), with 311 and 263 up- and downregulated respectively (Figure 1D and Suplementary files 1–2).
evidence: This is a direct result from the RNA-Seq analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Differentially expressed genes in neoplastic tumors include Matrix metalloprotease 1 (Mmp1), cheerio (cher), and insulin-like peptide 8 (Ilp8).
source: Differentially expressed genes include several previously identified neoplastic effectors, such as the pro-invasion factors Matrix metalloprotease 1 (Mmp1) and cheerio (cher) as well as the pupation regulator insulin-like peptide 8 (Ilp8) (Uhlirova and Bohmann, 2006; Colombani et al., 2012; Garelli et al., 2012; Külshammer and Uhlirova, 2013) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-Seq data and citations to prior research identifying these genes as neoplastic effectors.

claim: qRT-PCR analysis of differentially expressed genes shows close agreement with RNA-Seq data (R2 = 0.8844).
source: qRT-PCR analysis of these and other genes shows close agreement with RNA-Seq data (R2 = 0.8844).
evidence: This is a validation of the RNA-Seq data using an independent method.

claim: Upregulated genes in neoplastic tumors are enriched for factors involved in Response to Stimulus.
source: Amongst upregulated genes, Gene Ontology (GO) highlights factors involved in Response to Stimulus (Figure 1F,H).
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Several upregulated genes in neoplastic tumors are immune-related factors, which may be due to the recruitment of hemocytes to neoplastic tumors.
source: Several in this category are immune-related factors, and may be due to the recruitment of hemocytes to neoplastic tumors (Lebestky et al., 2000; Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008; Cordero et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the RNA-Seq data supported by citations to prior research on immune cell recruitment.

claim: 19 polarity-sensitive targets are also elevated in hyperoxic conditions.
source: Others, including Glutathione S transferase E1 (GstE1) and the chaperone CG7130, are regulated by oxidative stress, and overall 19 polarity-sensitive targets are also elevated in hyperoxic conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (Landis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the neoplastic transcriptome with published data on oxidative stress responses.

claim: Loss of dlg leads to higher superoxide levels, as evidenced by increased DHE staining.
source: Dihydroethidium (DHE), a fluorescent probe for superoxide anions, readily demonstrated elevation upon depletion of dlg (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is based on DHE staining experiments shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Co-overexpression of Catalase, Superoxide dismutase 2, or rat Glutathione Peroxidase 1 failed to alter the neoplastic phenotype induced by dlg knockdown.
source: Co-overexpression of Catalase, Superoxide dismutase 2, or rat Glutathione Peroxidase 1, which suppress other Drosophila ROS dependent phenotypes (Owusu-Ansah and Banerjee, 2009; Ohsawa et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2014) failed to alter the neoplastic phenotype induced by dlg knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F), although we were unable to detect a consistent reduction of DHE in these contexts.
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments testing the role of ROS in neoplastic growth.

claim: Primary GO categories among downregulated genes likely reflect the failure of neoplastic tumors to differentiate.
source: Primary GO categories among downregulated genes likely reflect the failure of neoplastic tumors to differentiate (Figure 1E,G,I).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Gene Ontology analysis of downregulated genes.

claim: Co-expression of vestigial (vg) suppressed dlgRNAi-induced overgrowth and architecture defects.
source: Strikingly, co-expression of vestigial (vg), a distal wing pouch selector that is downregulated in mutant discs, suppressed overgrowth and architecture defects (Figure 1J–M).
evidence: This is based on genetic rescue experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Vg overexpression eliminates polarity-deficient clones through apoptosis.
source: Though vg overexpression eliminates polarity-deficient clones through apoptosis (Khan et al., 2013), we recovered an intact wing pouch consisting of dlgRNAi/vg co-expressing cells (Figure 1M).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and contrasted with the current findings.

claim: Eyeless was incapable of suppressing dlg knockdown in wing or eye tissue.
source: eyeless was incapable of suppressing dlg knockdown in either context, but was also incapable of inducing broad photoreceptor differentiation in WT or dlg-depleted tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I, data not shown).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments testing the effect of ectopic eyeless expression.

claim: The JAK/STAT pathway is the only cell signaling pathway among the top GO categories in upregulated genes.
source: The only cell signaling pathway among the top GO categories is the JAK/STAT cascade.
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Upregulated genes in neoplastic tumors include STAT targets such as chinmo and Socs36E.
source: Upregulated genes include STAT targets such as chinmo and Socs36E, and a JAK/STAT activity reporter is strongly expressed in dlg and scrib discs (Figure 2A–B) (Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on the RNA-Seq data and reporter expression shown in Figure 2.

claim: A JAK/STAT activity reporter is strongly expressed in dlg and scrib discs.
source: Upregulated genes include STAT targets such as chinmo and Socs36E, and a JAK/STAT activity reporter is strongly expressed in dlg and scrib discs (Figure 2A–B) (Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on reporter expression shown in Figure 2.

claim: Each of the three unpaired (upd) genes were transcriptionally elevated between ∼3- and ∼50-fold in neoplastic tumors.
source: Remarkably, each of the three unpaired (upd) genes, which encode the ligands for the JAK/STAT pathway, were transcriptionally elevated between ∼3- and ∼50-fold, while genes encoding other signal transduction components were unaltered (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on the RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Genes encoding other JAK/STAT signal transduction components were unaltered in neoplastic tumors.
source: Remarkably, each of the three unpaired (upd) genes, which encode the ligands for the JAK/STAT pathway, were transcriptionally elevated between ∼3- and ∼50-fold, while genes encoding other signal transduction components were unaltered (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on the RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Socs36E decreased proliferation of dlghypo cells by 40%.
source: Strikingly, Socs36E decreased proliferation of dlghypo cells by 40%, while having no significant effect on growth or viability of WT discs (Figure 2D–H).
evidence: This is based on FACS-based quantification of cell numbers shown in Figure 2.

claim: Socs36E had no significant effect on growth or viability of WT discs.
source: Strikingly, Socs36E decreased proliferation of dlghypo cells by 40%, while having no significant effect on growth or viability of WT discs (Figure 2D–H).
evidence: This is based on FACS-based quantification of cell numbers shown in Figure 2.

claim: Expression of Socs36E or a dominant-negative form of Domeless (DomeDN) suppressed the growth of scrib-depleted discs.
source: Expression of Socs36E or a dominant-negative form of the JAK-STAT receptor Domeless (DomeDN) also suppressed the growth of scrib-depleted discs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The Scrib module regulates JAK-STAT ligand expression to suppress tissue overgrowth in imaginal discs.
source: We therefore conclude that in imaginal discs, as in RasV12-expressing clones (Wu et al., 2010), the Scrib module regulates JAK-STAT ligand expression to suppress tissue overgrowth.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional experiments and supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A 3 kb genomic DNA region surrounding the upd3 ATG was not expressed in WT discs but was distinctly upregulated in neoplastic discs.
source: We cloned 3 kilobases (kb) of genomic DNA surrounding the upd3 ATG into a lacZ reporter ('upd3lacZ') and found that this reporter was not expressed in WT discs. However, like the overlapping upd3 > GFP reporter, it was distinctly upregulated in neoplastic discs (Figure 3A–C) (Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on reporter expression experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: A 1-kb element within the first intron of upd3 (upd3.3LacZ) was expressed in a patchy manner throughout dlg discs.
source: Although reporters including upd3.1LacZ, which is activated by perturbations in the gut epithelium, remain silent, a 1-kb element within the first intron (upd3.3LacZ) was expressed in a patchy manner throughout dlg discs (Figure 3D–I).
evidence: This is based on reporter expression experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Expression of upd3.3lacZ was in cells of the disc proper, not in the peripodium or hemocytes.
source: Expression of upd3.3lacZ, like that of upd3lacZ, was in cells of the disc proper, not in the peripodium or hemocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B); this patchy expression resembled that seen with several other upregulated neoplastic effectors, (Figure 4B′, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–H).
evidence: This is based on microscopy analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Upd3.3LacZ was similarly activated in scrib discs.
source: Upd3.3LacZ was similarly activated in scrib discs, demonstrating that this enhancer is generally responsive to disruption of epithelial polarity (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E) and identifying a polarity-sensitive cis-regulatory region.
evidence: This is based on reporter expression experiments in scrib mutant discs.

claim: The upd3.3 enhancer contains two evolutionarily-conserved binding sites for AP-1, the Jun kinase (JNK) pathway transcription factor.
source: Motif scanning of the upd3.3 enhancer detected two evolutionarily-conserved binding sites for AP-1, the Jun kinase (JNK) pathway transcription factor (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,G).
evidence: This is based on computational motif scanning and evolutionary conservation analysis.

claim: Expression of a dominant-negative form of Drosophila JNK (JNKDN) blocks neoplastic overgrowth, as well as polarity and architecture defects.
source: Expression of a dominant-negative form of Drosophila JNK (Flybase: Basket), (JNKDN) has been shown to block neoplastic overgrowth, as well as polarity and architecture defects (Figure 4A–C,E–G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B) (Robinson and Moberg, 2011; Sun and Irvine, 2011).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in Figure 4 and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: JNKDN completely abrogated dlgRNAi-induced upd3.3LacZ expression.
source: Notably, JNKDN also completely abrogated dlgRNAi-induced upd3.3LacZ expression (Figure 4B′,C′; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), as well as that induced by scribRNAi (Figure 4—figure supplement 3G–H).
evidence: This is based on reporter expression experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutation of the JNK kinase, hemipterous (hep) prevented upd3.3LacZ levels in scrib tissue.
source: Mutation of the JNK kinase, hemipterous (hep) also prevented upd3.3LacZ levels in scrib tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D–F), confirming that canonical JNK signaling acts downstream of polarity disruption to regulate upd3.
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: fosDN fully phenocopied the effects of JNKDN: it prevented both upd3.3LacZ expression and dlgRNAi-mediated neoplasia.
source: Strikingly, fosDN fully phenocopied the effects of JNKDN: it prevented both upd3.3LacZ expression and dlgRNAi-mediated neoplasia (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Ectopic JNK activity in WT tissue leads to apoptosis.
source: Ectopic JNK activity in WT tissue leads to apoptosis (Igaki et al., 2002), so we co-expressed the JNK-activating ligand Eiger with a microRNA targeting the pro-apoptotic genes reaper, grim, and head involution defective (miRGH) to block both cell death and caspase activation (Siegrist et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: JNK activation alone induced upd3.3LacZ and increased tissue size.
source: In this context, JNK activation alone induced upd3.3LacZ (Figure 4H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C) and increased tissue size (Pérez-Garijo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: upd3.3LacZ induction by JNK activation alone was low compared to the canonical JNK target Mmp1.
source: However, upd3.3LacZ induction was low compared to the canonical JNK target Mmp1, while dlg knockdown activated both comparably (Figure 4B′,H).
evidence: This is based on comparison of reporter expression levels shown in Figure 4.

claim: JNK activation alone does not disrupt polarity.
source: Further, apical and basolateral proteins remained properly localized, indicating that JNK activation alone does not disrupt polarity (Figure 4I) (Sun and Irvine, 2011).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 4 and supported by citation.

claim: JNK signaling is sufficient for partial upd3.3 activation and overgrowth, but unable to induce full neoplasia.
source: Therefore, JNK signaling is sufficient for partial upd3.3 activation and overgrowth, but it is unable to induce full neoplasia.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experiments showing that JNK activation alone is insufficient to fully recapitulate the neoplastic phenotype.

claim: aPKC is strongly mislocalized upon loss of Scrib module function but not JNK activation.
source: One candidate is aPKC, which is strongly mislocalized upon loss of Scrib module function but not JNK activation (Figure 4F,I) (Bilder and Perrimon, 2000).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 4 and supported by citation.

claim: Constitutively active aPKC (aPKCact) was sufficient to potently trigger upd3.3LacZ transcription.
source: We expressed a constitutively active form (aPKCact) that can drive neoplasia and found that it was sufficient to potently trigger upd3.3LacZ transcription (Figure 5A; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on reporter expression experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: aPKCact can activate JNK targets.
source: aPKCact can also activate JNK targets (Figure 5A′), raising the possibility that aPKC regulates upd3 through JNK.
evidence: This is based on Mmp1 expression shown in Figure 5.

claim: Inhibiting JNK did not prevent aPKCact-mediated upd3.3LacZ activation or overgrowth, while it was effective at preventing expression of Mmp1.
source: However, inhibiting JNK did not prevent aPKCact-mediated upd3.3LacZ activation or overgrowth, while it was effective at preventing expression of Mmp1 (Figure 5B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: aPKC is capable of stimulating tumorigenic transcription independently of JNK.
source: Similar results were seen when membrane-bound WT aPKC (aPKCmild) was co-expressed with its partner Par-6, demonstrating that the results are not transgene-specific (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and thus showing that aPKC is capable of stimulating tumorigenic transcription independently of JNK.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on genetic experiments shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The upd3.3 enhancer contains a partially evolutionarily conserved binding site for Scalloped (Sd).
source: The enhancer contains a partially evolutionarily conserved binding site for Scalloped (Sd), a DNA-binding protein that recruits activated Yorkie (Yki) to target genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,H) (Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on computational motif scanning and evolutionary conservation analysis, supported by citation.

claim: Conserved Sd and AP-1 binding sites are found together in ∼1 kb regulatory regions of other upregulated genes.
source: Intriguingly, conserved Sd and AP-1 binding sites are also found together in ∼1 kb regulatory regions of other upregulated genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–F).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of regulatory regions shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Yki knockdown completely abrogated ectopic aPKC-driven upd3.3LacZ upregulation.
source: While yki knockdown under these conditions had a minimal effect on WT growth, it completely abrogated ectopic aPKC-driven upd3.3LacZ upregulation (Figure 5C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E; Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Depletion of yki suppressed the overgrowth of scrib tissue.
source: Similarly, depletion of yki suppressed the overgrowth of scrib tissue (Figure 4—figure supplement 3I–J).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Constitutively active Yki (Ykiact) displays massive overgrowth without affecting epithelial polarity.
source: We then analyzed discs overexpressing constitutively active Yki (Ykiact), which display massive overgrowth without affecting epithelial polarity (Dong et al., 2007; Oh and Irvine, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Upd3.3LacZ expression was highly elevated in Ykiact-expressing tissues.
source: Upd3.3LacZ expression was highly elevated in Ykiact-expressing tissues (Figure 5D–E; Figure 4—figure supplement 2C), indicating that Yki can also be sufficient to activate the polarity-responsive enhancer.
evidence: This is based on reporter expression experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Neither upd3.3lacZ nor JAK/STAT signaling was active in hyperproliferating hippo (hpo) pathway mutant tumors.
source: For instance, neither upd3.3lacZ nor JAK/STAT signaling was active in hyperproliferating hippo (hpo) pathway mutant tumors (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: This is based on reporter expression experiments shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Overexpression of either WT JNK kinase, or a membrane-targeted form of WT aPKC (aPKCmild), activated Mmp1 but does not cause substantial overgrowth and neither activates upd3.3lacZ.
source: Moreover, overexpression of either WT JNK kinase, or a membrane-targeted form of WT aPKC (aPKCmild), activated Mmp1 but does not cause substantial overgrowth; neither activates upd3.3lacZ (Figures 5F–G, 7J, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: Coexpression of JNK kinase and aPKCmild induced upd3.3lacZ upregulation, along with moderate overgrowth and polarity defects.
source: Strikingly, coexpression of JNK kinase and aPKCmild induced upd3.3lacZ upregulation (Figure 5H; Figure 4—figure supplement 2D), along with moderate overgrowth and polarity defects.
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: upd3.3 works as a 'coincidence detector', responding to simultaneous aPKC-mediated Yki activation and JNK-dependent Fos activation upon polarity loss.
source: These data support a model in which upd3.3 works as a 'coincidence detector', responding to simultaneous aPKC-mediated Yki activation and JNK-dependent Fos activation upon polarity loss.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the genetic experiments showing that both pathways are required for full enhancer activation.

claim: Mutations in PcG can result in tumorous growth.
source: Our previous work identified the upd genes as targets of direct repression by the Polycomb Group (PcG), and showed that mutations in PcG can result in tumorous growth (Classen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Imaginal discs mutant for the paralogous PcGs Psc and Su(z)2 show dramatic overgrowth, in which apicobasal polarity is often intact.
source: Imaginal discs mutant for the paralogous PcGs Psc and Su(z)2 show dramatic overgrowth, in which apicobasal polarity is often intact (Classen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Psc/Su(z)2 mutant discs upregulated upd3.3LacZ, but not other upd3LacZ subfragments.
source: Strikingly, they also upregulated upd3.3LacZ, but not other upd3LacZ subfragments (Figure 6B and data not shown).
evidence: This is based on reporter expression experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Nearly half of the genes upregulated upon polarity loss are also upregulated in PcG mutant tissues, a highly significant enrichment (p < 6.98e-121).
source: Comparison of Scrib module and PcG mutant RNA-Seq datasets revealed that nearly half of the genes upregulated upon polarity loss are also upregulated in PcG mutant tissues, a highly significant enrichment (p < 6.98e-121, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of RNA-Seq datasets shown in Figure 6.

claim: Nearly 25% of direct Pc-bound targets that are upregulated upon PcG loss are also upregulated in polarity-deficient tissues.
source: Further analysis of Scrib module transcriptomes revealed that nearly 25% of direct Pc-bound targets (Kwong et al., 2008) that are upregulated upon PcG loss are also upregulated in polarity-deficient tissues (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on comparison of RNA-Seq datasets with published ChIP data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: PcG mutant tissue often maintains polarized organization including areas that upregulate upd3.3lacZ.
source: An alternate possibility is that PcG mutant tissue itself is polarity-defective; however, it often maintains polarized organization including areas that upregulate upd3.3lacZ, it does not show transcriptional changes of polarity regulators, and unlike neoplastic tissue it is not suppressed by aPKC inhibition ([Classen et al., 2009], Figure 6—figure supplement 1, data not shown).
evidence: This is based on microscopy analysis and transcriptome data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Knockdown of ph-p alone has no effect on growth of WT discs.
source: Knockdown of the PcG gene polyhomeotic-proximal (ph-p) alone has no effect on growth of WT discs, due to the presence of its paralog polyhomeotic-distal (ph-d).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments and knowledge of genetic redundancy.

claim: Knockdown of ph-p in hypomorphic dlg discs significantly increased growth and cell proliferation.
source: However, when ph-p is knocked down in hypomorphic dlg discs, it significantly increased growth and cell proliferation (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: This is based on genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Expression of dominant-negative Brm reduced both the growth of dlgRNAi-expressing tissue and upd3.3LacZ expression.
source: We inhibited Brahma (Brm), which suppresses PcG-mediated homeotic transformation and often opposes PcG activity at target genes (Tamkun et al., 1992). Expression of dominant-negative Brm reduced both the growth of dlgRNAi-expressing tissue and upd3.3LacZ expression (Figure 7F–G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Expression of the core PcG components ph-p and Psc is reduced in neoplastic tumors to an extent similar to that seen upon strong JNK activation.
source: Expression of the core PcG components ph-p and Psc is reduced in neoplastic tumors to an extent similar to that seen upon strong JNK activation (Figure 7H), suggesting that JNK signaling upon polarity loss compromises PcG function.
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Upon knockdown of ph-p, mild aPKC signaling drove robust overgrowth and upd3.3LacZ upregulation.
source: However, upon knockdown of ph-p, which does not activate JNK, mild aPKC signaling not only drove robust overgrowth but also upd3.3LacZ upregulation (Figure 7I–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Epithelial polarity normally suppresses neoplasia through PcG in cooperation with JNK and aPKC/Yki pathways.
source: From these data, we conclude that epithelial polarity normally suppresses neoplasia through PcG in cooperation with JNK and aPKC/Yki pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic interaction experiments.

claim: In polarity-deficient tissues, the simultaneous initiation of Fos-dependent transcription, aPKC-mediated Yki activation, and loss of PcG target repression leads to induction of a broad group of oncogenic factors, including the mitogenic JAK/STAT ligands.
source: In polarity-deficient tissues, the simultaneous initiation of Fos-dependent transcription, aPKC-mediated Yki activation, and loss of PcG target repression leads to induction of a broad group of oncogenic factors, including the mitogenic JAK/STAT ligands.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition of Fos can suppress upd3 upregulation and neoplasia.
source: Inhibition of Fos can suppress upd3 upregulation and neoplasia, indicating that this transcription factor itself is the major target of JNK in this context.
evidence: This is based on the genetic experiments showing that FosDN suppresses neoplasia.

claim: A polarity-sensitive enhancer is not fully activated by JNK alone, even when apoptosis is blocked.
source: Yet a polarity-sensitive enhancer is not fully activated by JNK alone, even when apoptosis is blocked.
evidence: This is based on the experiments showing that JNK activation with apoptosis blocked only partially activates upd3.3.

claim: aPKC can activate Yki independent of, rather than through, JNK.
source: aPKC is an additional regulator of this enhancer, and as previously suggested (Doggett et al., 2011), can activate Yki independent of, rather than through, JNK.
evidence: This is based on the genetic experiments and supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Inhibiting either the JNK or Hpo pathways, including depletion of the downstream transcription factors, prevents expression of the polarity-sensitive enhancer.
source: Inhibiting either the JNK or Hpo pathways, including depletion of the downstream transcription factors, prevents expression of the polarity-sensitive enhancer; our analysis predicts that mutating transcription factor binding sites would give the same effect.
evidence: This is based on the genetic experiments showing that both pathways are required.

claim: Knockdown of upd3 alone in neoplastic tumors does not prevent overgrowth.
source: Knockdown of upd3 alone in neoplastic tumors does not prevent overgrowth (Figure 2—figure supplement 1); upd1 and upd2 are also regulated by JNK, Yki, and PcG (Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008; Classen et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2009; Staley and Irvine, 2010; Wu et al., 2010) and may act through analogous enhancers to cooperatively drive tumor formation.
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Loss of polarity induces two separate signaling pathways: JNK to induce Fos-dependent transcription, and mispolarization of aPKC drives Yki-dependent transcription.
source: Loss of polarity thus induces two separate signaling pathways. An unknown mechanism triggers JNK to induce Fos-dependent transcription, while at the same time mispolarization of aPKC drives Yki-dependent transcription.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanistic findings.

claim: Under mild signaling conditions, both JNK/Fos and aPKC/Yki pathways are required simultaneously to trigger enhancer expression or overgrowth.
source: Under mild signaling conditions, both pathways are required simultaneously to trigger enhancer expression or overgrowth, while inhibition of either is sufficient to suppress neoplasia.
evidence: This is based on the genetic experiments showing coincidence detection.

claim: Polarity-responsive enhancers like upd3.3 work as 'coincidence detectors' that during normal physiology require inputs from both JNK/Fos and aPKC/Yki.
source: We suggest that polarity-responsive enhancers like upd3.3 work as 'coincidence detectors' that during normal physiology require inputs from both JNK/Fos and aPKC/Yki.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Inhibition of Fos can revert not only growth defects but also polarity defects of neoplastic tumors.
source: Our results also emphasize the unexpectedly central role of transcription in mediating cell polarity loss. Inhibition of Fos can revert not only growth defects but also polarity defects of neoplastic tumors.
evidence: This is based on the genetic experiments showing that FosDN restores polarity.

claim: Activation of JNK, Yki, or both together is insufficient to elicit polarity defects.
source: Nevertheless, activation of JNK, Yki, or both together is insufficient to elicit polarity defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), while aPKC activation alone is.
evidence: This is based on genetic experiments shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Many Hpo pathway targets, including direct growth regulators such as cycE, diap1, and Myc, are expressed at near-normal levels in Scrib module mutants.
source: Many Hpo pathway targets, including direct growth regulators such as cycE, diap1, and Myc, are expressed at near-normal levels in Scrib module mutants, and comparison of Scrib module and Hpo mutant transcriptomes reveals limited overlap (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is based on the RNA-Seq data and transcriptome comparisons shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: A transgenic 3.5 kb diap1 fragment is strongly upregulated in neoplastic tissue, paralleling upregulation of a minimal Yki-responsive element.
source: It is also unlikely to be explained by a model in which Yki activation through aPKC differs from Yki activation through canonical Hpo pathway regulators, since a transgenic 3.5 kb diap1 fragment is strongly upregulated in neoplastic tissue, paralleling upregulation of a minimal Yki-responsive element (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G–J).
evidence: This is based on reporter expression experiments shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: An enhancer trap inserted at the same 3.5 kb sequence in the endogenous diap1 locus is only slightly upregulated in neoplastic tissue.
source: Interestingly, an enhancer trap inserted at the same 3.5 kb sequence in the endogenous diap1 locus (Zhang et al., 2008) is only slightly upregulated by comparison (Figure 5—figure supplement 2K–L), hinting that the native chromatin environment at certain Yki targets might influence target response.
evidence: This is based on reporter expression experiments shown in the supplementary figure and supported by citation.

claim: Canonical PcG targets including Hox genes are not upregulated in neoplastic tissues.
source: However, since canonical PcG targets including Hox genes are not upregulated in neoplastic tissues (Supplementary files 1–2), and overall Histone H3K27me3 levels are not altered (data not shown), the data rule out a global inactivation of PcG.
evidence: This is based on the RNA-Seq data and histone modification analysis.

claim: Overall Histone H3K27me3 levels are not altered in neoplastic tissues.
source: However, since canonical PcG targets including Hox genes are not upregulated in neoplastic tissues (Supplementary files 1–2), and overall Histone H3K27me3 levels are not altered (data not shown), the data rule out a global inactivation of PcG.
evidence: This is based on histone modification analysis.

claim: Decreased PcG-mediated repression 'primes' select targets for activation by polarity-responsive effector pathways.
source: Instead, they suggest that decreased PcG-mediated repression 'primes' select targets for activation by polarity-responsive effector pathways.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the genetic interaction data.

claim: Reduced PcG activity upon Scrib module loss synergizes with JNK and aPKC signaling, perhaps by providing a permissive chromatin environment for Fos- and Yki-stimulated transcription.
source: Mild activation of either JNK or aPKC alone is insufficient to stimulate enhancers such as upd3.3. However, at these targets, reduced PcG activity upon Scrib module loss synergizes with JNK and aPKC signaling, perhaps by providing a permissive chromatin environment for Fos- and Yki-stimulated transcription.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the genetic interaction data.

claim: Fly homologs of metabolic genes that fuel human cancer growth are elevated in neoplastic tumors, including fatty acid synthase (FASN) and LDH.
source: In addition to oxidative stress, fly homologs of metabolic genes that fuel human cancer growth are elevated, including fatty acid synthase (FASN) which facilitates de novo lipogenesis, and LDH which promotes aerobic glycolysis in the Warburg effect (Cairns et al., 2011; Baenke et al., 2013; Gorrini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on the RNA-Seq data and supported by citations to research on cancer metabolism.

claim: Glycolytic enzyme transcription in fly neoplastic tumors remains relatively unchanged.
source: However, glycolytic enzyme transcription in fly neoplastic tumors remains relatively unchanged, suggesting that metabolic changes may be more complex.
evidence: This is based on the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Restoring expression of the wing-fate regulator Vg suppresses tumorous overgrowth without inducing cell death.
source: Khan et al. recently reported that forcing differentiation can cause elimination of neoplastic clones (Khan et al., 2013); by contrast, our experiments show that restoring expression of the wing-fate regulator Vg suppresses tumorous overgrowth without inducing cell death.
evidence: This is based on the genetic experiments with vg overexpression and contrasted with prior research.

claim: Apicobasal polarity disruption elicits responses with striking parallels to those seen in epithelial wounds in both Drosophila and humans.
source: Why might loss of polarity drive this particular constellation of events that result in tumorous overgrowth? Our global analysis reveals that apicobasal polarity disruption elicits responses with striking parallels to those seen in epithelial wounds in both Drosophila and humans (Schäfer and Werner, 2008; Lee and Miura, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the transcriptome data supported by citations to wound healing research.

claim: Several upregulated neoplastic effectors that contain conserved AP-1 and Sd binding sites are also upregulated during wound-healing.
source: Intriguingly, several upregulated neoplastic effectors that contain conserved AP-1 and Sd binding sites are also upregulated during wound-healing (Pastor-Pareja et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2009; Garelli et al., 2012; Patterson et al., 2013) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the neoplastic transcriptome with published wound healing data.

claim: Linking transcriptional control of wound-response targets to polarity regulators allows the tissue to connect disturbances in its integrity to the activation of broad gene expression programs that promote repair.
source: An attractive model is that linking transcriptional control of such targets to polarity regulators, via polarity-regulated aPKC, cell architecture-regulated Yki and stress-regulated JNK activity on both downstream transcription factors and PcG epigenetic regulators, allows the tissue to connect disturbances in its integrity to the activation of broad gene expression programs that promote repair.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Following tissue damage, restoration of tissue architecture and integrity would abrogate wound-response signals.
source: Following tissue damage, restoration of tissue architecture and integrity would abrogate wound-response signals.
evidence: This is a logical inference about normal wound healing.

claim: In polarity-deficient tissues, architecture can never be restored, and pro-growth, de-differentiation cues remain active, leading to the formation of malignant tumors that kill the organism.
source: In contrast, in polarity-deficient tissues, architecture can never be restored, and these pro-growth, de-differentiation cues remain active, leading to the formation of malignant tumors that kill the organism.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of why polarity loss leads to neoplasia.

claim: The data provide insight into why epithelial polarity is tumor-suppressive by linking it to cancers as 'wounds that never heal'.
source: Our data linking apicobasal polarity to neoplastic gene expression thus suggest an evolutionarily ancient genesis for cancers as 'wounds that never heal' (Dvorak, 1986).
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the findings supported by citation to the 'wounds that never heal' concept.
